title: Go: From Zero to Backend
summary:
A guided, hands-on course in Go that takes you from your very first line of code
to the ideas that power real backend services. You read a short concept, build
muscle memory by typing small, complete programs with the tutor — every line
explained — and then apply what you learned in a graded challenge whose hidden
tests decide correctness. Twenty-six units of steadily rising difficulty: printing
with fmt, variables and types, control flow, loops, functions with multiple
returns, your own structs and methods, interfaces, slices and maps, error
handling, and the Go module system (go get); an intermediate database track built
on SQLite through database/sql and the pure-Go modernc.org/sqlite driver —
connecting and querying, transactions, the connection pool and WAL mode, the N+1
query problem, pagination, and indexes with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN; then an advanced
concurrency track —
goroutines and WaitGroups, channels, select with timeouts, and shared state with
mutexes and worker pools; and a data structures & algorithms track: stacks and
queues, linked lists, maps and sets, binary search trees, sorting and searching,
and recursion with dynamic programming. Almost everything runs on the standard
library; two exercises teach you how to pull in and run an external package the
way every real Go project does. No prior Go needed.
overview:
## What Go is

Go is a statically typed, compiled programming language created at Google and released as open source in 2009. It was designed for large teams building networked software: the syntax is small, the compiler is fast, and a program compiles to a single native binary that you can copy to a server and run. The standard library ships with what a backend needs out of the box, from HTTP servers to JSON encoding.

## Where it is used

Go is a mainstay of cloud infrastructure. Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus are all written in Go, and many companies use it for backend services and APIs, command-line tools and developer tooling. If you work near containers, DevOps or web backends, you will meet Go code.

## The mental model this course builds

- **Simplicity.** Go has few keywords and usually one obvious way to do something: one loop keyword, no classes, no inheritance.
- **Composition through interfaces.** You describe behaviour with small interfaces, and any type that has the right methods fits them automatically.
- **Errors as values.** There are no exceptions. A function that can fail returns an `error`, and you check it with `if err != nil`.
- **Goroutines and channels.** Concurrency is built in: you start lightweight goroutines with `go` and let them communicate over channels.

## How the course is organised

The **Basic** units cover printing with `fmt`, variables and types, `if`/`switch`, the `for` loop and functions with multiple returns. The **Intermediate** units add structs and methods, interfaces, slices and maps, errors, a first look at goroutines and the module system (`go get`), then a database track on SQLite using `database/sql`: queries, transactions, the connection pool and WAL mode, the N+1 problem, pagination and indexes. The **Advanced** units go deep into concurrency (`sync.WaitGroup`, channels, `select` with timeouts, mutexes and worker pools) and then data structures and algorithms: stacks, queues, linked lists, sets, binary search trees, sorting, searching, recursion and dynamic programming.

## How each unit works

Every unit has three kinds of step. A **concept** step explains one idea in a few paragraphs. A **drill** has you retype a short, complete program line by line, with each line explained, so the shape of the code goes into your fingers. A **challenge** asks you to implement a function on your own; hidden tests, run with `go test`, decide whether it is correct.

units.concepts:
## The idea

A computer does not understand English; it executes machine instructions, one after another. A **programming language** is a precise notation that humans can read and that a tool can translate into those instructions. Go is a **compiled** language: the Go toolchain reads your source code, checks it, and produces a native program (a **binary**) that the operating system can run directly.

Every program needs an agreed starting point, called the **entry point**. It also needs a way to talk to the outside world. The simplest channel is **standard output** (stdout): a stream of text that the terminal displays. Printing to stdout is how your first programs show their results.

Programs are also built from reusable pieces. Code that someone else has already written and organised under a name is a **package**. Go comes with a large **standard library** of packages, and `fmt` (short for "format") is the one for printing text.

## How Go does it

A runnable program lives in `package main` and starts at `func main()`. You `import` the packages you use and call their functions with the `package.Function` notation.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("first line")
    fmt.Println("second line", 42)
}
```

`fmt.Println` prints its arguments separated by spaces and adds a newline. `fmt.Printf` gives you control: its first argument is a **format string** with **verbs** that are replaced, in order, by the remaining arguments. `%s` takes a string, `%d` an integer, and `%v` takes any value in its default form.

```go
city := "Luanda"
fmt.Printf("%s has %d letters\n", city, 6)
```

Text in double quotes is a **string**. You can join two strings with `+`: `"Good " + "morning"` produces `"Good morning"`. A function can also take input (parameters) and hand a value back with `return`; you will write one in the challenge and study functions properly in unit 5.

## What is special or tricky

- **Go is strict about unused things.** Importing `fmt` and never using it is a compile error: `"fmt" imported and not used`. The same applies to local variables you declare but never read.
- **Exported names start with a capital letter.** It is `fmt.Println`, never `fmt.println`; the lowercase spelling does not compile, because lowercase names are private to their package.
- **`Printf` adds no newline.** Forget the `\n` and the next output continues on the same line.
- **A missing argument is not a compile error.** `fmt.Printf("%d\n")` still builds, then prints `%!d(MISSING)`. Run `go vet` and it will catch this.
- **The opening brace stays on the same line** as `func main()`. Go inserts semicolons automatically at line ends, so a `{` on its own line breaks the code.
- **Use `gofmt`.** Go has one official layout, and editors apply it automatically, so all Go code looks alike.

## What you will practise

You will type the classic first program and a `Printf` line with `%s` and `%d`, then write your first function, one that builds a greeting string from a name it receives.
units.title: Hello & fmt
units.intro:
Your very first steps in Go: what a program is, how to print to the screen with
the `fmt` package, and how the compiler turns your text into a running binary. By
the end you will write a tiny greeting function and let the hidden tests check it.

steps.title: What a Go program is
steps.intro:
Before you write anything, picture what a computer actually does: it loads a
compiled program into memory and executes machine instructions one after another.
A program needs one agreed place to begin — in Go that place is the function
`main`, inside the special `package main`. The Go toolchain compiles your source
into a native binary; when you run it, the operating system hands control to
`main`, and anything you print travels to **standard output**, which the terminal
shows on screen.
steps.body:
## A program starts at `main`

Every runnable Go program lives in **`package main`** and begins at a function
called **`main`**. Think of `main` as the front door: when you run the program,
Go walks in through `main` and does, top to bottom, whatever it finds there.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello, Go!")
}
```

Four things to notice:

- **`package main`** marks this file as a buildable command (not a library).
- **`import "fmt"`** pulls in the standard-library `fmt` package, which formats
  and prints text.
- **`func main() { ... }`** declares the entry point; the `{ }` hold its body.
- **`fmt.Println(...)`** prints a line of text, then a newline, to standard output.

You compile and run a single-file program with **`go run .`**. In the next steps
you will type small, complete programs yourself; when your code matches the
target, the tutor runs it so you can see the output.

steps.title: Print your first line
steps.intro:
This drill cements the one skeleton every Go program shares. `fmt.Println` writes
your text to standard output and adds a trailing newline. There is no loop and no
branching here — just the entry point `main` and a single write to the screen.
steps.prompt:
Type the classic first program. It prints a single line and stops.

**Why:** this cements the shape every Go program shares — `package main`, an
`import`, and a `main` that writes one line. Reproduce it exactly.
line_comments: Declares this file as part of `package main` — the special package that builds a runnable command.
Imports the standard-library `fmt` package, which formats and prints text.
Declares `main`, the function Go runs first; `{` opens its body.
Prints the text followed by a newline to standard output.
Closes the body of `main`; when execution reaches here the program ends.
steps.explanation:
That is a complete Go program. Go entered `main`, ran the one `fmt.Println`,
printed `Hello, Go!`, and then `main` ended — so the program finished. Every
program you write grows from exactly this skeleton.

steps.title: Format with Printf
steps.intro:
`fmt.Println` prints values as-is; `fmt.Printf` lets you build a formatted string
with **verbs**: `%s` for a string, `%d` for an integer. Unlike `Println`, `Printf`
does not add a newline for you, so you write `\n` yourself where you want one.
steps.prompt:
Use `fmt.Printf` with the `%s` and `%d` verbs to interpolate a name and a number
into one line. Note the explicit `\n` at the end.
line_comments: Declares `name` and infers its type (string) with the short form `:=`.
`Printf` fills `%s` with `name` and `%d` with `15`; `\n` ends the line.
steps.explanation:
`Printf` is the workhorse of formatted output: each verb (`%s`, `%d`, ...) is
replaced, left to right, by the matching argument. Because `Printf` prints exactly
what you give it, you control the newline with `\n`.

steps.title: Implement Greet
steps.intro:
Now you apply what you learned. In Go, strings join with the `+` operator, and a
function declares what it returns after its parameter list. Your function takes a
`string` and returns a new `string`. Hidden tests, not the screen, decide
correctness.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `Greet`:

```go
func Greet(name string) string { ... }
```

It takes a name and returns a string that reads `Hello, {name}!`.

Examples:

- `Greet("World")` → `"Hello, World!"`
- `Greet("Go")` → `"Hello, Go!"`

**Hint:** build the result by joining strings with `+`.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
Joining strings copies the fixed text `Hello, ` and `!` plus the `n` characters of
`name` into a fresh string. Both the work and the memory grow in direct proportion
to the length of `name`, so the time is **O(n)** and the space is **O(n)**, where
`n` is the length of the name. There is no hidden loop — a single pass builds the
result once.

units.concepts:
## The idea

A program works with **values**: numbers, pieces of text, true or false. To keep a value around and refer to it later, you give it a name. That named storage location is a **variable**. Each value also has a **type**, which says what kind of data it is and which operations make sense on it. You can add two numbers, but adding a number to the word "hello" means nothing.

Languages differ in when they check types. Go is **statically typed**: every variable has one type that is fixed at **compile time**, before the program runs. If you misuse a type, the compiler refuses to build the program, so many bugs never reach your users. The trade-off is that you must sometimes say exactly what you mean, for example when mixing whole and fractional numbers.

## How Go does it

The basic types you will use most are `int` (whole numbers), `float64` (numbers with a fractional part), `string` (text) and `bool` (`true` or `false`). There are two ways to declare a variable:

```go
var score int = 90       // explicit type
var name string          // no value: gets the zero value ""
ratio := 0.75            // short form: type inferred as float64
```

The short form `:=` works only inside functions and infers the type from the value: `7` becomes an `int`, `2.5` a `float64`. You change an existing variable with plain `=`.

Every type has a **zero value** that a variable gets when you don't initialise it: `0` for numbers, `""` for strings, `false` for booleans. Go never leaves memory uninitialised.

Converting between numeric types is always explicit, written like a function call:

```go
km := 42
miles := float64(km) * 0.621371
whole := int(miles)      // drops the fraction: 26
```

## What is special or tricky

- **No implicit conversion.** If `rate` is a `float64` variable, `km * rate` fails with `invalid operation: km * rate (mismatched types int and float64)`. Go makes you choose the conversion so the rounding behaviour is visible.
- **Integer division truncates.** `7 / 2` is `3`, not `3.5`. This includes constants: `1 / 2` is `0`, while `1.0 / 2` is `0.5`. Watch the order of operations in a formula when integers are involved.
- **Converting to `int` truncates toward zero**; it does not round. `int(2.9)` is `2`.
- **`:=` declares, `=` assigns.** Using `:=` again for a name that already exists in the same scope gives `no new variables on left side of :=`. Assigning with `=` to a name never declared gives `undefined`.
- **Unused variables are errors**: `declared and not used: x`.
- **A variable's type never changes.** Assigning a string to an `int` variable is a compile error.

## What you will practise

You will declare variables with both `var` and `:=`, convert an `int` to `float64` before multiplying, and then write a function that applies a temperature formula entirely in `float64`.
units.title: Variables & types
units.intro:
Every value in Go has a **type** the compiler tracks for you: whole numbers
(`int`), real numbers (`float64`), text (`string`), truth values (`bool`). You
will meet the two ways to declare a variable (`var` and the short `:=`) and see
why Go makes you convert between numeric types on purpose.

steps.title: Values, types and declarations
steps.intro:
A variable is a named box in memory holding a value of a fixed type. Go is
statically typed: the type is known at compile time, which lets the compiler catch
mistakes before the program ever runs.
steps.body:
## Two ways to declare

```go
var age int = 15   // explicit type
city := "Luanda"   // short form: type inferred as string
```

- **`var name type = value`** states the type explicitly.
- **`name := value`** is the short form (only inside functions); Go **infers** the
  type from the value.

Go's basic types include `int`, `float64`, `bool`, and `string`. Unlike some
languages, Go will **not** silently mix numeric types: to multiply an `int` by a
`float64` you must convert, e.g. `float64(count) * price`. That explicitness
prevents a whole class of rounding bugs.

steps.title: Declare with var and :=
steps.intro:
Both declaration forms store a typed value. `var age int = 15` is explicit; the
short `city := "Luanda"` infers `string`. Printing several values with `Println`
separates them with spaces.
steps.prompt: Declare one variable with `var` and one with `:=`, then print them.
steps.target:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    var age int = 15
    city := "Luanda"
    fmt.Println(age, city)
}
line_comments: Declares `age` as an `int` with the explicit `var` form.
Declares `city` with the short `:=` form; its type is inferred as string.
Prints both values, separated by a space.
steps.explanation:
`var` and `:=` both create a typed variable — `:=` just lets the compiler infer
the type. Inside functions the short form is the idiomatic choice.

steps.title: Convert between number types
steps.intro:
Go will not mix an `int` and a `float64` automatically. To multiply them you
convert the `int` with `float64(...)` first. This drill shows that explicit
conversion.
steps.prompt:
Multiply an integer count by a floating-point price. Convert the `int` to
`float64` before the multiplication.
steps.target:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    count := 7
    price := 2.5
    total := float64(count) * price
    fmt.Println("Total:", total)
}
line_comments: `price` is inferred as `float64` because it has a decimal point.
Converts `count` to `float64` so the multiplication type-checks.
Prints a label and the computed total.
steps.explanation:
The compiler rejects `count * price` because the types differ. `float64(count)`
makes the conversion explicit and the intent obvious — Go never guesses for you.

steps.title: Implement CelsiusToFahrenheit
steps.intro:
Apply numeric types and arithmetic. The formula is `F = C * 9/5 + 32`. Because you
work entirely in `float64`, no conversion is needed inside the function — the
caller passes a `float64` and you return one.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `CelsiusToFahrenheit`:

```go
func CelsiusToFahrenheit(c float64) float64 { ... }
```

It converts a temperature in Celsius to Fahrenheit using `F = C * 9/5 + 32`.

Examples:

- `CelsiusToFahrenheit(0)` → `32`
- `CelsiusToFahrenheit(100)` → `212`
- `CelsiusToFahrenheit(-40)` → `-40`

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The function performs a fixed number of arithmetic operations — one multiply, one
divide, one add — regardless of the input value. There is no loop and no allocation
that grows with the input, so both the time and the space are **O(1)** (constant).

units.concepts:
## The idea

So far, programs ran every line from top to bottom. Real programs must **decide**: grant access or refuse it, charge shipping or not. **Control flow** is the order in which statements execute, and a **branch** is a point where the program picks one path out of several based on a **condition**.

A condition is a **boolean expression**: an expression whose result is either `true` or `false`. You build them with comparison operators (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) and combine them with logical operators: `&&` (and), `||` (or), `!` (not). `&&` and `||` **short-circuit**: if the left side already decides the answer, the right side is not evaluated.

## How Go does it

`if` runs a block when its condition is `true`. An optional `else if` chain tests further conditions in order, and `else` catches everything left over. Exactly one block runs.

```go
if temp > 30 {
    fmt.Println("hot")
} else if temp > 15 {
    fmt.Println("mild")
} else {
    fmt.Println("cold")
}
```

`switch` compares one value against several `case` labels. A case can list several values, and `default` handles the rest. A `switch` with no value after the keyword tests a boolean expression in each case and takes the first one that is true, a tidy replacement for a long `else if` chain:

```go
switch {
case score >= 90:
    fmt.Println("A")
case score >= 75:
    fmt.Println("B")
default:
    fmt.Println("keep practising")
}
```

An `if` can also start with a short statement whose variable lives only inside the `if`/`else`. For example, `if r := n % 3; r == 0 { ... }` computes `r` and tests it in one line.

## What is special or tricky

- **The condition must be a real `bool`.** Some languages treat `0` or an empty string as false; Go does not. `if n { }` with an `int` fails with `non-boolean condition in if statement`.
- **No parentheses, but braces are mandatory.** Even a one-line body needs `{ }`, and `else` must sit on the same line as the closing `}` of the `if`. Otherwise the automatically inserted semicolon ends the `if` early and you get a syntax error.
- **No fall-through in `switch`.** After the first matching case runs, the `switch` ends. You rarely need `break`; the `fallthrough` keyword exists but is seldom used.
- **Case order matters** in a tagless `switch` and in `else if` chains: the first true condition wins, so test the narrowest condition first.
- **`=` is not `==`.** Writing `if x = 5` is rejected by the compiler, which saves you from a classic bug.

## What you will practise

You will branch on whether a number is even with `if`/`else` and `%`, map numbers to day names with a `switch`, and then write a function that classifies an integer into one of three categories.
units.title: Control flow (if / switch)
units.intro:
Programs make decisions. You will use `if`/`else` to branch on a boolean condition
and `switch` to pick cleanly among several cases. By the end you classify a number
in a graded challenge.

steps.title: Branching with if and switch
steps.intro:
A branch lets the program take one path or another depending on a condition
evaluated at run time. Go's `if` needs no parentheses around the condition, and
its `switch` does not fall through by default — each case stands alone.
steps.body:
## `if` / `else`

```go
if n%2 == 0 {
    fmt.Println("even")
} else {
    fmt.Println("odd")
}
```

The condition must be a `bool`. No parentheses are required; the braces are.

## `switch`

```go
switch day {
case 1:
    fmt.Println("Monday")
case 3:
    fmt.Println("Wednesday")
default:
    fmt.Println("Other")
}
```

Unlike C, Go does **not** fall through from one case to the next, so you rarely
need `break`. A `switch` with many cases reads far more clearly than a long chain
of `else if`.

steps.title: Branch with if/else
steps.intro:
`%` is the remainder operator. `n%2 == 0` is true exactly when `n` is even, so this
`if`/`else` prints one word or the other.
steps.prompt: Use `if`/`else` and the `%` operator to print whether a number is even or odd.
line_comments: If the remainder of `n` divided by 2 is zero, `n` is even.
Prints `odd` when `n` is not divisible by 2.
steps.explanation:
The condition `n%2 == 0` is a `bool`; Go runs the matching block and skips the
other. Change `n` and the branch taken changes with it.

steps.title: Choose with switch
steps.intro:
`switch` compares one value against several `case` labels and runs the first that
matches, with no fall-through. `default` handles everything else.
steps.prompt: Map a day number to a day name with a `switch`, including a `default`.
line_comments: Printed when `day == 3` — our value, so this runs.
steps.explanation:
Go runs exactly one matching case and then leaves the `switch` — no `break`
needed. Because `day` is 3, only `Wednesday` prints.

steps.title: Implement Sign
steps.intro:
Apply branching. You classify an integer as negative, zero, or positive and return
the matching word. Either an `if`/`else if`/`else` chain or a `switch` works.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `Sign`:

```go
func Sign(n int) string { ... }
```

Return `"negative"` when `n < 0`, `"zero"` when `n == 0`, and `"positive"` when
`n > 0`.

Examples:

- `Sign(-5)` → `"negative"`
- `Sign(0)` → `"zero"`
- `Sign(42)` → `"positive"`

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
The function checks at most two comparisons and returns — the number of operations
does not depend on how large `n` is. No loop, no allocation that grows with input,
so both time and space are **O(1)**.

units.concepts:
## The idea

**Iteration** means repeating a block of code: once per item in a list, until a condition changes, or a fixed number of times. A **loop** has a body, which is the code being repeated, and a rule for when to stop. Each pass through the body is one iteration.

A common pattern inside a loop is the **accumulator**: a variable that starts with a neutral value (`0` for a sum, `1` for a product, an empty string for text) and is updated on every iteration. When the loop ends, the accumulator holds the answer.

Loops also introduce **cost**. A loop that runs once per item does work proportional to the input size; in **Big-O** notation that is **O(n)**. A loop nested inside another loop over the same data is **O(n²)**. This tells you how a program slows down as the data grows.

## How Go does it

Go has a single loop keyword, `for`, used in several shapes:

```go
for i := 10; i > 0; i -= 2 {   // init; condition; post
    fmt.Println(i)              // 10 8 6 4 2
}

n := 100
for n > 1 {                     // while-style: condition only
    n = n / 2
}
```

With no condition at all, `for { ... }` loops forever until a `break` (leave the loop) or a `return`. `continue` skips the rest of the current iteration and moves on to the next one.

`range` walks a collection and gives you the index and a copy of the element. Since Go 1.22 you can also range over an integer to repeat something a fixed number of times:

```go
names := []string{"Ana", "Bo"}
for i, name := range names {
    fmt.Println(i, name)
}
for i := range 3 {              // i = 0, 1, 2
    fmt.Println("lap", i)
}
```

Use the blank identifier `_` to ignore a value you don't need: `for _, name := range names`.

## What is special or tricky

- **There is no `while` keyword** and no `do`/`while`; `for` covers both.
- **Off-by-one errors** are the classic loop bug. Decide whether the bound is inclusive (`<=`) or exclusive (`<`), and test the smallest inputs, such as zero and one.
- **Edge cases:** if the condition is false at the start, the body runs zero times. That is often exactly what you want for empty or non-positive input.
- **Infinite loops** happen when the condition never becomes false, for example when you forget to change the loop variable.
- **`range` gives copies.** Assigning to `v` inside `for _, v := range nums` does not change the slice.
- **Unused loop variables are errors.** If you don't need the index, write `_` instead of `i`, or the compiler reports `declared and not used`.

## What you will practise

You will add up a fixed range with a classic counting loop, walk a slice with `range`, and then write a function that accumulates a total over a range whose end comes from its argument, including what happens when that argument is zero or negative.
units.title: Loops (for)
units.intro:
Repetition is where computers shine. Go has exactly one loop keyword — `for` — that
plays every role: counting loop, while-style loop, and range loop over a collection.
By the end you sum the numbers up to `n` in a graded challenge.

steps.title: The one loop: for
steps.intro:
A loop repeats a block while a condition holds. Go unifies all looping into the
single keyword `for`, so there is less to remember and one shape to master.
steps.body:
## Three shapes, one keyword

```go
for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ {   // classic counter: init; condition; post
    sum += i
}

for condition {             // while-style
    // ...
}

for i, v := range nums {    // range over a slice/map/string
    fmt.Println(i, v)
}
```

- The **classic** form has three parts: an initializer, a condition, and a
  post-statement (`i++`).
- Drop the init and post to get a **while** loop.
- **`range`** walks a collection, handing you the index and the value each turn.

Loop cost matters: a single `for` over `n` items is **O(n)**; a loop inside a loop
is **O(n²)**. You will meet that idea again when complexity is graded.

steps.title: Count with a for loop
steps.intro:
The classic three-part `for` runs its body once per value of `i`, from 1 through 5,
accumulating the running total in `sum`.
steps.prompt: Add the numbers 1 through 5 with a classic `for` loop and print the total.
line_comments: Starts the running total at zero.
Loops `i` from 1 while `i <= 5`, adding 1 each turn (`i++`).
Adds the current `i` to `sum` (`+=` means `sum = sum + i`).
steps.explanation:
The loop body runs five times, once for each `i` in 1..5, and `sum` grows to 15.
One pass over `n` items is linear — **O(n)** work.

steps.title: Walk a slice with range
steps.intro:
`range` over a slice yields the index and the value on each turn. It is the
idiomatic way to visit every element without managing an index by hand.

units.concepts:
## The idea

A **function** is a named, reusable piece of work. It receives inputs through **parameters**, runs its body, and hands results back to the **caller** with `return`. Functions let you break a big problem into small pieces you can understand and test one at a time, a principle called **decomposition**. The function's **signature** (its name, parameter types and result types) is a contract: callers only need to know the signature, not how the body works.

When you call a function, Go evaluates the **arguments** and copies them into the parameters. This is **pass by value**: the function works on its own copies, so changing a parameter inside the function does not change the caller's variable.

Many languages let a function return only one value. Go lets a function return **several**, which removes the need for special wrapper objects and makes the result of an operation easy to read at the call site.

## How Go does it

Parameters are written `name type`, and adjacent parameters of the same type can share it: `(a, b int)`. Result types follow the parameter list; several results go in parentheses.

```go
func area(w, h float64) float64 {
    return w * h
}

func sumAndProduct(a, b int) (int, int) {
    return a + b, a * b
}

s, p := sumAndProduct(3, 4)   // s = 7, p = 12
_, p2 := sumAndProduct(2, 5)  // ignore the first result
```

Results can also be **named**, which documents what each one means. Named results start at their zero values, and a bare `return` sends back their current values:

```go
func split(total int) (half, rest int) {
    half = total / 2
    rest = total - half
    return
}
```

Functions can be declared in any order in a file; `main` can call a helper defined below it.

## What is special or tricky

- **The caller must take every result.** `x := sumAndProduct(1, 2)` fails with `assignment mismatch: 1 variable but sumAndProduct returns 2 values`. Use `_` to discard a result you don't need.
- **Every path must return.** If a function has results and some path can reach the closing brace without a `return`, the compiler reports `missing return`.
- **Integer `/` and `%` truncate toward zero.** `7 / 2` is `3` and `7 % 2` is `1`; with negatives, `-7 / 2` is `-3` and `-7 % 2` is `-1`. Dividing an integer by zero causes a runtime **panic**: `integer divide by zero`.
- **Bare returns hurt readability** in long functions. Use them only in very short ones.
- **The `(value, error)` shape** you see across the standard library is simply a two-result function. You will build on it in the errors unit.

## What you will practise

You will write and call a one-result helper, unpack a function that returns two values in order, and then implement a function that returns two related results of integer arithmetic at once.

units.concepts:
## The idea

Real programs model things: a user, an order, a rectangle. Each thing has several pieces of data that belong together. A **composite type** bundles those pieces into one value. In Go that type is the **struct**: a fixed set of named, typed **fields**.

Data is only half of the model; the other half is **behaviour**, the operations that make sense for that data. A **method** is a function attached to a type. It receives the value it operates on as a special parameter called the **receiver**. Keeping data and its behaviour together is the core idea of **encapsulation**, and Go gets it without classes or inheritance.

## How Go does it

You declare a struct with `type Name struct { ... }`, build values with a **composite literal**, and read or change fields with the dot operator. A method is declared with the receiver in parentheses before its name.

```go
type Book struct {
    Title string
    Pages int
}

func (b Book) IsLong() bool {
    return b.Pages > 400
}

b := Book{Title: "Dune", Pages: 612}
fmt.Println(b.Title, b.IsLong())   // Dune true
```

Fields you leave out of a literal get their zero values, so `Book{}` has an empty title and zero pages. You can also define a named type over a basic type (`type Celsius float64`) and give it methods.

A receiver can be a **value** (`b Book`), in which case the method gets a copy, or a **pointer** (`c *Counter`), in which case the method can modify the original:

```go
type Counter struct{ n int }

func (c *Counter) Inc() { c.n++ }

var c Counter
c.Inc()          // Go takes &c for you
fmt.Println(c.n) // 1
```

## What is special or tricky

- **Capital letters control visibility.** `Title` and `IsLong` are **exported** and visible from other packages; a lowercase `n` is private to its package. There are no `public` or `private` keywords.
- **Value receivers work on a copy.** A method with a value receiver that assigns to a field changes only the copy, and the caller sees no change. That is a silent bug, not a compile error. Use a pointer receiver when a method must modify the value.
- **Structs are copied on assignment.** `b2 := b` creates an independent copy; changing `b2.Pages` leaves `b` alone.
- **Mistyped fields are caught.** A typo such as `b.Pagez` gives `b.Pagez undefined (type Book has no field or method Pagez)`. In a literal, an unknown field name gives `unknown field`.
- **Positional literals** like `Book{"Dune", 612}` must list every field in order. Prefer named fields: they survive field reordering and are self-documenting.
- **Methods must be declared in the same package as the type.** You cannot add methods to `int` or to types from another package.

## What you will practise

You will define a struct and read its fields, attach a method to a named numeric type, and then define a struct of your own with a method that computes a value from its fields.
units.title: Structs & methods

steps.title: Your own types
steps.intro:
A struct is a composite type: several typed fields bundled under one name. A method
is a function with a **receiver** — the value it acts on — written just before the
name. Together they are how Go models data and the behaviour that belongs with it.
steps.body:
## Struct + method

```go
type Rectangle struct {
    Width  float64
    Height float64
}

func (r Rectangle) Area() float64 {
    return r.Width * r.Height
}
```

- Create a value with `Rectangle{Width: 3, Height: 4}` and read a field with
  `r.Width`.
- **`func (r Rectangle) Area() float64`** adds a method; `r` is the receiver, the
  specific rectangle the method runs on. Call it with `r.Area()`.

Capitalised names (`Width`, `Area`) are **exported** — visible from other packages;
lowercase names are private to the package. That single rule is Go's whole access
model.

units.concepts:
## The idea

Most programs handle collections of data. Two **data structures** cover the vast majority of cases.

A **dynamic array** stores elements of one type in a **contiguous** block of memory, in order. Reading element `i` is **O(1)** because its address can be computed directly. When the array is full, a bigger block is allocated and the elements are copied over. Because the capacity grows geometrically, adding at the end is **amortised O(1)**.

A **hash table** stores **key→value** pairs. A **hash function** turns each key into a bucket position, so looking up, inserting or deleting a key takes **O(1) on average**, no matter how many entries there are. Hash tables are the standard tool for counting, grouping, caching and removing duplicates.

## How Go does it

Go's dynamic array is the **slice**. A slice is a small header that points to an underlying **backing array** and records a length (`len`) and a capacity (`cap`). You grow a slice with `append` and take sub-slices with `s[low:high]`, where `high` is exclusive:

```go
fruits := []string{"apple", "pear"}
fruits = append(fruits, "fig", "kiwi")
fmt.Println(len(fruits), fruits[1:3])   // 4 [pear fig]
```

Go's hash table is the **map**, written `map[KeyType]ValueType`. Reading a missing key returns the value type's zero value. The **comma-ok** form tells you whether the key was really present, and `delete` removes a key:

```go
capitals := make(map[string]string)
capitals["Angola"] = "Luanda"
city, ok := capitals["Peru"]          // city == "", ok == false
delete(capitals, "Angola")
for country, c := range capitals {   // order is not specified
    fmt.Println(country, c)
}
```

`make(map[K]V)` creates an empty, ready-to-use map; a literal like `map[string]int{"a": 1}` creates and fills one.

## What is special or tricky

- **Always assign `append` back.** `append` may allocate a new backing array and return a new header. Calling `append(s, x)` as a bare statement is a compile error (`is not used`), and dropping the result loses the element.
- **Sub-slices share memory.** `t := s[0:2]` points into the same backing array, so writing `t[0]` changes `s[0]` too.
- **Out-of-range indexes panic** at run time: `index out of range [5] with length 3`.
- **A nil map can be read but not written.** `var m map[string]int` declares a nil map; `m["x"] = 1` panics with `assignment to entry in nil map`. Create maps with `make` or a literal.
- **Map iteration order is randomised** and differs between runs. Never rely on it; sort the keys if you need a stable order.
- **A missing key is not an error.** `m[k]` quietly returns the zero value, which is handy for counters but can hide typos. Use comma-ok when you need to tell absent from zero.

## What you will practise

You will grow a slice with `append` and check its `len`, build and query a map, and then combine the two: walk a slice once and build a map that summarises it.
units.title: Slices & maps
units.intro:
Two collections power almost every Go program: the **slice** (a growable, ordered
list) and the **map** (a key→value lookup table). By the end you count how many
times each word appears — a tiny search index.

steps.title: Slices and maps
steps.intro:
A slice is a view over a contiguous, growable array of elements of one type. A map
stores key→value pairs with average constant-time lookup via hashing. Between them
they cover ordered lists and keyed lookups.
steps.body:
## Slice

```go
nums := []int{1, 2, 3}
nums = append(nums, 4)   // grows the slice
fmt.Println(len(nums))   // 4
```

`append` returns a (possibly new) slice, so you assign it back. `len` reports the
length.

## Map

```go
ages := map[string]int{"Ana": 30}
ages["Bo"] = 25             // insert
fmt.Println(ages["Ana"])    // 30

n, ok := ages["Zed"]        // ok is false when the key is absent
```

A map lookup is **O(1)** on average — that is why maps are the go-to tool for
counting, grouping, and de-duplicating. The comma-ok form (`n, ok := m[k]`) tells
you whether the key existed.

units.concepts:
## The idea

Things go wrong: a file is missing, the input is invalid, the network is down. A language needs a way to signal **failure** and let the caller decide what to do. Many languages use **exceptions**, which jump out of the current function and unwind the call stack until some handler catches them. That is convenient, but the failure path is invisible at the call site.

Go takes another approach: **errors are values**. A function that can fail returns an extra result of type `error`, and the caller checks it right away. Every failure path is visible in the code, and handling an error is ordinary control flow with `if`, nothing magical.

## How Go does it

`error` is a built-in interface with a single method, `Error() string`. By convention it is the **last** result, and `nil` means success. When there is an error, the other results are usually zero values that the caller should ignore.

```go
var ErrInsufficient = errors.New("insufficient funds")

func withdraw(balance, amount int) (int, error) {
    if amount > balance {
        return balance, ErrInsufficient
    }
    return balance - amount, nil
}

left, err := withdraw(50, 80)
if err != nil {
    fmt.Println("cannot withdraw:", err)
    return
}
fmt.Println("left:", left)
```

`errors.New` builds a simple error. A package-level error variable like `ErrInsufficient` is called a **sentinel error**: a known value that callers can compare against.

As an error travels up the call stack, each layer can add context by **wrapping** it with `fmt.Errorf` and the `%w` verb. `errors.Is` then searches the whole chain:

```go
err := fmt.Errorf("pay invoice 42: %w", ErrInsufficient)
fmt.Println(err)                             // pay invoice 42: insufficient funds
fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, ErrInsufficient)) // true
```

## What is special or tricky

- **Check the error first, then use the value.** Using a result before testing `err` is a common bug; when `err != nil`, the other results are not meaningful.
- **Don't ignore errors.** Writing `v, _ := f()` throws the error away. The compiler allows it, but it hides failures. If you assign `err` and never read it, the compiler reports `declared and not used`.
- **`%w` versus `%v`.** `%v` only copies the message text; `%w` keeps the original error inside, so `errors.Is` can still find it. Compare with `==` only when you know the error was not wrapped.
- **Error strings are lowercase with no final punctuation**, because they are often embedded in longer messages: `"open config: file not found"`.
- **`panic` is not for ordinary failures.** It is reserved for truly unexpected states, such as a program bug. Dividing an integer by zero triggers a runtime panic, which is why code that divides by user input should check the divisor first and return an error instead.

## What you will practise

You will return an error or `nil` from a validation function, wrap a sentinel error with `%w` and detect it with `errors.Is`, and then write a function with the canonical `(result, error)` signature that refuses a bad input instead of crashing.

units.concepts:
## The idea

**Concurrency** means structuring a program as several tasks that make progress independently, such as serving many requests at once or downloading files while the interface stays responsive. **Parallelism** is running tasks at literally the same instant on several CPU cores. Concurrency is about structure; parallelism is one possible outcome of it.

Concurrent tasks need to **communicate** and **synchronise**, which means waiting for one another at the right moment. Go follows the idea of **communicating sequential processes**: rather than many tasks poking at the same memory, they pass values to one another through channels. A Go proverb puts it this way: do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.

Programs also build on code written by others. A **dependency manager** records which external **modules** a project uses and at which exact versions, so builds are reproducible.

## How Go does it

A **goroutine** is a function running concurrently, started with the `go` keyword. Goroutines are scheduled by the Go runtime onto OS threads and are cheap enough to start by the thousands. A **channel**, made with `make(chan T)`, is a typed pipe: `ch <- v` sends, `<-ch` receives. On an unbuffered channel the sender blocks until a receiver is ready, and the receiver blocks until a value is sent.

```go
results := make(chan string)
for _, name := range []string{"db", "cache"} {
    go func() { results <- name + " ok" }()
}
fmt.Println(<-results)
fmt.Println(<-results)  // two sends, two receives
```

A `sync.WaitGroup` waits for a group of goroutines: `Add(1)` before starting each one, `defer wg.Done()` inside it, and `Wait()` to block until all are done. A sender can `close(ch)` to signal that no more values are coming; then `for v := range ch` receives until the channel is closed and empty.

Modules: `go get github.com/google/uuid` adds a dependency to `go.mod` and records checksums in `go.sum`; then you `import` it and `go run .` as usual. `go mod tidy` adds missing requirements and removes unused ones.

## What is special or tricky

- **When `main` returns, the program exits**, even if goroutines are still running. You must wait for them with a channel receive or a `WaitGroup`.
- **Deadlock.** Receiving from a channel that no one will ever send on, or sending with no receiver, blocks forever. If every goroutine is stuck, the runtime stops with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`.
- **Scheduling order is not deterministic.** Output from several goroutines can appear in any order. Design results that do not depend on order.
- **Data races.** Several goroutines writing the same variable without synchronisation corrupt it; concurrent map writes crash with `fatal error: concurrent map writes`. `go run -race` detects races. Prefer channels here; mutexes come in a later unit.
- **Loop variables.** Since Go 1.22 each iteration gets its own copy, so closures capture the right value. Passing it as an argument, as older code does, is still correct.

## What you will practise

You will hand a value from a goroutine to `main` over a channel, wait for several workers with a `WaitGroup`, install and use two external packages with `go get`, and then compute a result using goroutines whose answer must not depend on scheduling.
units.title: Goroutines, channels & packages
units.intro:
The two things real Go backends lean on most: lightweight **concurrency**
(goroutines, channels, `sync.WaitGroup`) and the **module system** that pulls in
other people's code with `go get`. You will run concurrent work, coordinate it, use
two popular external packages, and finish by summing a slice concurrently.

steps.title: Goroutines, channels, and go get
steps.intro:
A goroutine is a function running concurrently, scheduled by the Go runtime on top
of OS threads — cheap enough to launch thousands. Channels pass values safely
between goroutines. And when your program needs code it did not write, the module
system fetches it with `go get`.
steps.body:
## Goroutines & channels

```go
done := make(chan string)   // a channel of strings
go func() {                 // launch a goroutine
    done <- "finished"      // send on the channel
}()
msg := <-done               // receive (blocks until a value arrives)
```

- **`go f()`** runs `f` concurrently and returns immediately.
- A **channel** (`make(chan T)`) is a typed pipe; `ch <- v` sends, `<-ch` receives.
- Receiving **blocks** until a value is ready, which is how goroutines synchronise.

## Waiting for many: sync.WaitGroup

```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() { defer wg.Done(); work() }()
}
wg.Wait()   // blocks until all three call Done
```

## Pulling in packages with go get

Real services use libraries. You add one to your module and download it with:

```sh
go get github.com/google/uuid
```

Then `import "github.com/google/uuid"` and run with `go run .`. The toolchain
records the dependency in `go.mod` and its exact version in `go.sum`. The next two
drills do exactly this with two well-known packages — watch the tutor show you the
install command.

steps.title: Launch a goroutine, use a channel
steps.intro:
A goroutine runs the anonymous function concurrently; it sends a message on the
channel, and `main` blocks on the receive until that value arrives — a clean
hand-off between concurrent work and the main flow.

steps.title: Coordinate with sync.WaitGroup
steps.intro:
A `sync.WaitGroup` counts outstanding goroutines. Each `Add(1)` before launching,
each `Done()` as it finishes, and `Wait()` blocks until the count returns to zero —
so `main` does not exit before the workers do.

Registers one more goroutine with the group.

`defer` guarantees `Done` runs when the goroutine returns.

Blocks until all three workers have called `Done`.
Prints a final line after everyone finished.
steps.explanation:
`Add`/`Done`/`Wait` are the counter that lets `main` wait for concurrent work.
Passing `i` as an argument gives each goroutine its own copy. Worker lines may print
in any order — that is concurrency.

steps.title: Implement SumConcurrent
steps.intro:
Tie it together. You sum a slice of integers using concurrency: launch goroutines
that each report a partial result over a channel, then combine them. The answer must
be deterministic even though the work runs concurrently — the sum of a set does not
depend on the order you add it.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `SumConcurrent`:

```go
func SumConcurrent(nums []int) int { ... }
```

Return the sum of all the integers in `nums`, computed with the help of goroutines
and a channel (or a `sync.WaitGroup`). The result must be correct and deterministic
regardless of goroutine scheduling.

Examples:

- `SumConcurrent([]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5})` → `15`
- `SumConcurrent(nil)` → `0`

**Hint:** send each number (or a partial sum) on a channel and add up everything
you receive. Addition is commutative, so order does not matter.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
Each of the `n` numbers is handled by one goroutine that sends on the channel, and
the collector receives `n` values, so the work is **O(n)**. The buffered channel
holds up to `n` pending values, so the extra space is **O(n)**. Because addition is
commutative, the total is the same no matter which goroutine is scheduled first,
which keeps the result deterministic.

units.concepts:
## The idea

A relational database stores data in **tables**: rows of records that all share the same named columns. You talk to it in **SQL**, a declarative language: you describe *what* you want (`SELECT name FROM users WHERE age > 30`) and the database's query planner decides *how* to get it. Statements come in two families: those that change things and return no rows (`CREATE TABLE`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`), and queries that return a **result set** of rows.

SQLite is an **embedded** database: there is no server process. The whole engine is a library inside your program, and a database is a single file, or with `:memory:` a scratch database in RAM.

The most important habit is how values get into SQL. Gluing input into the query text, as in `"... WHERE name = '" + name + "'"`, lets the input change the *structure* of the query: a name like `x' OR 1=1 --` turns a lookup into "return every row". That is **SQL injection**. A **placeholder** (`?`) fixes the shape of the statement first and sends the values separately, as data that is never parsed as SQL.

## How Go does it

Go splits the job in two. The standard package `database/sql` defines one API, and a **driver** implements it for a particular database. This course uses `modernc.org/sqlite`, a pure-Go driver that registers itself under the name `sqlite` when it is imported. You import it only for that side effect, with a blank import (`_`).

Three calls cover most work: `Exec` for statements without rows, `QueryRow` for exactly one row, and `Query` for many rows. Arguments after the SQL fill the `?` placeholders in order.

```go
// Safe: title is bound to ?, never parsed as SQL.
db.Exec(`INSERT INTO books (title, year) VALUES (?, ?)`, title, 1999)
```

`Query` returns a `*sql.Rows` cursor. You advance it with `Next` and copy columns into variables with `Scan`, passing pointers:

```go
rows, err := db.Query(`SELECT title FROM books WHERE year < ?`, 2000)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer rows.Close()
for rows.Next() {
    var title string
    if err := rows.Scan(&title); err != nil {
        return err
    }
    fmt.Println(title)
}
return rows.Err()
```

## What is special or tricky

- Forget the blank import and you get, at run time, `sql: unknown driver "sqlite" (forgotten import?)`. Import it without `_` and the compiler says it is imported and not used.
- `sql.Open` does not necessarily connect; it prepares a handle. Problems such as a bad path often surface at the first `Exec` or `Query`.
- `Scan` wants pointers, one per selected column. A mismatch gives `sql: expected 2 destination arguments in Scan, not 1`.
- When `QueryRow` finds no row, `Scan` returns `sql.ErrNoRows` and leaves your variable untouched.
- Always `defer rows.Close()`: an unclosed cursor keeps hold of a connection. Check `rows.Err()` after the loop.
- Placeholders stand for values only. `SELECT * FROM ?` cannot choose a table.
- The drills discard errors with `_` to stay short; real code checks every one.

## What you will practise

You will open an in-memory database, insert rows with placeholders, read a single value with `QueryRow` and loop over results with `Query`. The challenge asks you to let SQL, not a Go loop, do the counting.
units.title: Databases: connect & query
units.intro:
Real services keep their state in a database. Go talks to SQL databases through the
standard `database/sql` package plus a driver. Here you use SQLite with the pure-Go
driver `modernc.org/sqlite` (no C compiler needed): open a database, create a table,
insert rows with `?` placeholders, and read them back with `QueryRow` and `Query`.

steps.title: database/sql and a driver
steps.intro:
`database/sql` is a thin, driver-agnostic layer. You import a driver for its side
effect (a blank import) so it registers itself, then open a handle by the driver's
registered name.
steps.body:
## Open, exec, query

```go
import (
    "database/sql"

    _ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
defer db.Close()

db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER, name TEXT)`)
db.Exec(`INSERT INTO users VALUES (?, ?)`, 1, "Ana")

var n int
db.QueryRow(`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users`).Scan(&n)
```

- The **blank import** `_ "modernc.org/sqlite"` registers the driver named `sqlite`.
- **`sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")`** returns a `*sql.DB` handle — a pool, not a
  single connection.
- **`Exec`** runs statements that return no rows; **`?`** placeholders bind values
  safely (never build SQL by string concatenation).
- **`QueryRow(...).Scan(&n)`** reads exactly one row into Go variables.

For many rows, use `Query` and loop with `rows.Next()` / `rows.Scan(...)`, and always
`defer rows.Close()`.

steps.title: Open, create, count
steps.intro:
Open an in-memory SQLite database, create a table, insert one row, and count the
rows. The driver is registered by the blank import; `:memory:` is a throwaway
database that lives only while the program runs.

`COUNT(*)`.

`sql.Open` hands you a pool; `Exec` runs statements; `QueryRow(...).Scan` reads one

steps.title: QueryRow with a placeholder
steps.intro:
`QueryRow` plus a bound `?` fetches a single value for a single key — the everyday
lookup. Insert two people, then read one person's age back by name.

Insert two rows, then use `QueryRow(... WHERE name = ?, "Ana").Scan(&age)` and print
the age.

Will hold the age we look up.

A bound parameter (`?`) is matched positionally with the argument you pass after the

steps.title: Loop over many rows
steps.intro:
When a query returns several rows you iterate with `rows.Next()` and `rows.Scan()`.
`ORDER BY` makes the output deterministic. Remember to `defer rows.Close()`.
steps.prompt:
Insert three numbers, `Query` them `ORDER BY x`, sum them in a `rows.Next()` loop,
and print the total.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE nums (x INTEGER)`)
	db.Exec(`INSERT INTO nums VALUES (10), (20), (30)`)
	rows, _ := db.Query(`SELECT x FROM nums ORDER BY x`)
	defer rows.Close()
	total := 0
	for rows.Next() {
		var x int
		rows.Scan(&x)
		total += x
	}
	fmt.Println(total)
}

Runs a query that returns many rows, ordered for determinism.
Closes the row set when done.
Running total of the scanned values.
Advances to the next row until there are none.
steps.explanation:
`Query` returns a cursor; each `Next()` advances it and `Scan` reads the current row.
Ordering the query keeps the printed result stable run to run.

steps.title: Implement CountAdults
steps.intro:
Put the query pattern to work. You receive rows of `(name, age)` as `[][2]any`,
insert them into a table, and return how many people are adults — counted by SQL,
not by a Go loop.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `CountAdults`:

```go
func CountAdults(rows [][2]any) int { ... }
```

Each element is `[2]any{name, age}`. Open an in-memory database, create a table,
insert every row with `?` placeholders, and return `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE
age >= 18`.

Examples:

- `CountAdults([][2]any{{"Ana", 30}, {"Bo", 17}})` -> `1`
- `CountAdults(nil)` -> `0`

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
Each of the `n` input rows is inserted once, so the work and the stored rows both
grow linearly: **O(n)** time and **O(n)** space. The `COUNT(*)` with a `WHERE` runs
inside SQLite; the boundary `age >= 18` is handled by the database, not Go.

units.concepts:
## The idea

Many real operations need several writes that only make sense together. Moving money is the classic case: subtract from one account, add to the other. If the program crashes or hits an error between the two, money has vanished. A **transaction** groups statements into one unit of work with the **ACID** properties:

- **Atomicity**: all the statements take effect, or none do.
- **Consistency**: the database moves from one valid state to another.
- **Isolation**: other connections never see the half-finished work, only the state before or after.
- **Durability**: once committed, the change survives a crash or power loss.

You **begin** a transaction, run statements, then either **commit** (publish everything at once) or **roll back** (discard everything). Without an explicit transaction, SQLite runs each statement in its own tiny transaction, a mode called **autocommit**.

A side benefit: the commit is the expensive part, because the database must flush to disk. A thousand inserts in one transaction are far faster than a thousand autocommits.

## How Go does it

`db.Begin()` reserves one connection from the pool and returns a `*sql.Tx`. A `Tx` has the same `Exec`, `Query` and `QueryRow` methods as `*sql.DB`, but they all run on that reserved connection, inside the transaction. `Commit` or `Rollback` ends it and hands the connection back.

The idiomatic shape defers a rollback right after `Begin`. If the function returns early with an error, the deferred call undoes the work. If `Commit` ran first, the later `Rollback` does nothing except return `sql.ErrTxDone`, which you ignore.

```go
func addOrder(db *sql.DB, customer string, items []string) error {
    tx, err := db.Begin()
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer tx.Rollback()

    res, err := tx.Exec(`INSERT INTO orders (customer) VALUES (?)`, customer)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    orderID, _ := res.LastInsertId()
    for _, it := range items {
        _, err := tx.Exec(`INSERT INTO lines (order_id, item) VALUES (?, ?)`, orderID, it)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return tx.Commit()
}
```

Either the order and all of its lines exist, or none of them does.

## What is special or tricky

- Run the statements on `tx`, not on `db`. A call on `db` borrows a *different* connection outside the transaction: it does not see the uncommitted work and is not undone by a rollback.
- With `:memory:` this bites harder: every SQLite connection to `:memory:` gets its own private database. While a transaction holds one connection, a query on `db` may open a second one and find no tables at all.
- Rolling back is not only for errors. Your code may decide that a business rule was broken and roll back on purpose. Inside the transaction, its own uncommitted changes are visible to its own queries.
- `Commit` returns an error; check it. A failed commit means nothing was saved.
- After `Commit` or `Rollback` the `Tx` is finished; further calls fail with `sql: transaction has already been committed or rolled back`.
- Forgetting to end a transaction leaks its connection and can hold a lock that blocks other writers.

## What you will practise

You will commit a row, roll another back and watch it vanish, and move money between two accounts in a single transaction. The challenge adds a rule that makes your code choose between `Commit` and `Rollback` at run time.
units.title: Transactions: all or nothing
units.intro:
A transaction groups several statements so they either all take effect or none do.
You use `db.Begin()` to start one, run statements on the returned `*sql.Tx`, then
`Commit()` to keep the changes or `Rollback()` to discard them. You will build a
money transfer that rolls back rather than leave an account negative.

steps.title: Begin, Commit, Rollback
steps.intro:
Without a transaction, each statement commits on its own — a crash halfway leaves
inconsistent data. A transaction makes a group of statements atomic.
steps.body:
## The transaction shape

```go
tx, err := db.Begin()
if err != nil {
    return err
}
tx.Exec(`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = 1`, amount)
tx.Exec(`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = 2`, amount)

if bad {
    tx.Rollback() // undo everything in this tx
    return nil
}
tx.Commit() // make it permanent
```

- **`db.Begin()`** returns a `*sql.Tx`; run your statements on `tx`, not `db`.
- **`tx.Commit()`** makes every change in the transaction permanent at once.
- **`tx.Rollback()`** throws the whole group away — the database looks as if nothing
  happened.
- A transfer is the classic example: debit and credit must both succeed, or neither.

steps.title: Commit keeps the change
steps.intro:
Begin a transaction, insert a row, and `Commit`. After committing, the row is really
there — the count is 1.
steps.prompt: Inside a transaction insert one row, `Commit`, then print `COUNT(*)`.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER)`)
	tx, _ := db.Begin()
	tx.Exec(`INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)`)
	tx.Commit()
	var n int
	db.QueryRow(`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t`).Scan(&n)
	fmt.Println(n)
}
line_comments: ...plus the pure-Go `modernc.org/sqlite` driver, blank-imported so it registers itself under the name `sqlite`.
Inserts a row inside the transaction.
Counts the rows after the commit.
Prints 1 — the committed row is there.
steps.explanation:
Statements run on the `*sql.Tx`. `Commit` publishes them; a later read on the `db`
handle sees the committed row.

steps.title: Rollback undoes the change
steps.intro:
Same insert, but call `Rollback` instead of `Commit`. The insert is discarded, so the
count is 0 — proof that nothing in a rolled-back transaction survives.
steps.prompt: Inside a transaction insert one row, `Rollback`, then print `COUNT(*)`.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER)`)
	tx, _ := db.Begin()
	tx.Exec(`INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)`)
	tx.Rollback()
	var n int
	db.QueryRow(`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t`).Scan(&n)
	fmt.Println(n)
}
line_comments: ...plus the pure-Go `modernc.org/sqlite` driver, blank-imported so it registers itself under the name `sqlite`.
Inserts a row inside the transaction.
Rolls back, discarding everything the transaction did.
Counts the rows after the rollback.
Prints 0 — the rolled-back insert left no trace.
steps.explanation:
`Rollback` discards every change made since `Begin`. The row never becomes visible,
so the count stays at 0.

steps.title: Two updates, one commit
steps.intro:
A transfer is two updates that must land together. Debit one account and credit
another inside a single transaction, commit, and read the destination balance.
steps.prompt:
Seed two accounts, in one transaction move 40 from account 1 to account 2, commit,
and print account 2's balance.
steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE acct (id INTEGER, bal INTEGER)`)
	db.Exec(`INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 100), (2, 0)`)
	tx, _ := db.Begin()
	tx.Exec(`UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 40 WHERE id = 1`)
	tx.Exec(`UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 40 WHERE id = 2`)
	tx.Commit()
	var b int
	db.QueryRow(`SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 2`).Scan(&b)
	fmt.Println(b)
}

Creates an `acct` table with an id and a balance.
Seeds account 1 with 100 and account 2 with 0.
Begins a transaction so both updates land together.
Reads account 2's balance after the commit.
steps.explanation:
Both `UPDATE`s run inside the same transaction, so `Commit` applies them atomically.
Account 2 ends with the 40 that left account 1.

steps.title: Implement Transfer
steps.intro:
Make the transfer safe. Move `amount` from A to B inside one transaction; if either
balance would end up negative, roll the whole thing back and report the original
balances unchanged.

space are **O(1)**. Atomicity comes from the transaction: on the overdraw path the

units.concepts:
## The idea

Opening a database connection is relatively costly, and one connection can serve only one statement at a time. Services therefore keep a **connection pool**: a set of open connections lent to whoever needs one and returned afterwards. The pool reuses idle connections, opens new ones on demand, and can cap how many exist.

Concurrency also raises a storage question: how do readers and writers share one file safely? SQLite's default **rollback journal** copies each page's original content to a side file before changing it, so a crash can be undone. While a writer commits, readers are locked out.

**Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)** flips this around. Changes are appended to a separate `-wal` file instead of overwriting the main database. A reader looks at the main file plus the WAL up to the moment its read began, a consistent **snapshot**, so readers do not block the writer and the writer does not block readers. Now and then a **checkpoint** copies the logged pages back into the main file. There is still only **one writer at a time**: a second writer must wait for the lock.

## How Go does it

`*sql.DB` *is* the pool. It is safe for concurrent use by many goroutines: each `Exec` or `Query` borrows a connection, runs, and gives it back. You create one `*sql.DB` for the whole program and share it.

```go
db, err := sql.Open("sqlite", "file:app.db?_pragma=busy_timeout(5000)")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
db.SetMaxOpenConns(4) // never more than 4 connections
db.SetMaxIdleConns(4) // keep them around for reuse
db.SetConnMaxLifetime(time.Hour)
```

The `modernc.org/sqlite` driver reads `_pragma=` options from the DSN (the connection string) and applies them to every new connection it opens. `busy_timeout(5000)` makes a connection wait up to five seconds for a lock instead of failing at once.

WAL is switched on with a pragma, which also returns the resulting mode:

```go
var mode string
db.QueryRow(`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`).Scan(&mode) // "wal"
```

## What is special or tricky

- Most pragmas affect only the **connection** that runs them. `db.Exec` of `PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000` configures one pooled connection, and the next statement may run on another. That is why per-connection settings belong in the DSN. `journal_mode=WAL` is the exception: it is stored in the database file and persists.
- WAL needs a real file. On `:memory:` the pragma reports `memory`, and each pooled connection would get its own separate in-memory database anyway.
- Without a busy timeout, concurrent writers fail with `database is locked` (`SQLITE_BUSY`).
- `SetMaxOpenConns(0)`, the default, means unlimited. With a cap, a goroutine that asks for a connection while all are busy simply waits.
- Never open a pool per goroutine or per request: you lose reuse and multiply file handles.
- Wait for the workers (a `sync.WaitGroup` is the usual tool) before reading the result, and try `go run -race .` to catch data races in your own Go code.
- A WAL database keeps `-wal` and `-shm` files beside it. They are part of the database; do not delete them while it is in use.

## What you will practise

You will switch a file-backed database to WAL, cap the pool, and have several goroutines insert through one shared `*sql.DB`. The challenge asks for a result that is the same however the goroutines happen to be scheduled.
units.title: WAL mode & the connection pool
units.intro:
`*sql.DB` is a pool of connections, not a single wire — safe to share across
goroutines. SQLite's Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode lets readers and a writer work
concurrently. Here you turn on WAL, cap the pool with `SetMaxOpenConns`, and have
several goroutines insert through the shared pool to a deterministic total.

steps.title: A pool you can share
steps.intro:
`sql.Open` returns a pool. Goroutines can call it concurrently; the pool hands each
one a free connection. WAL mode improves read/write concurrency on SQLite.
steps.body:
## Pool and WAL

```go
db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", "file:app.db")
db.SetMaxOpenConns(4) // at most 4 live connections

db.Exec(`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`) // readers don't block the writer

var wg sync.WaitGroup
for w := 0; w < 4; w++ {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()
        db.Exec(`INSERT INTO nums VALUES (?)`, 1)
    }()
}
wg.Wait()
```

- **`*sql.DB` is safe for concurrent use** — share the one handle, never open a pool
  per goroutine.
- **`SetMaxOpenConns(n)`** bounds how many connections exist at once.
- **WAL** (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`) needs a real file, not `:memory:`, and lets
  reads proceed while a write is in flight.
- A **busy timeout** makes a connection wait briefly for a lock instead of failing
  immediately — add it to the DSN so every pooled connection inherits it.

units.concepts:
## The idea

Every statement sent to a database has a fixed cost on top of the actual work: the request travels to the server, the SQL is parsed and planned, and the result travels back. That is a **round trip**. Over a network it often costs around a millisecond, far more than finding a few rows in an index.

The **N+1 problem** appears when code first runs one query to get a list (the "1"), then loops over the list and runs one more query per item (the "N"). With 3 items nobody notices. With 10 000 items, a page that runs 10 001 queries takes seconds, and the database spends most of its time on overhead. It often hides inside helper functions or ORMs that load related records lazily, so each query looks innocent on its own.

The fix is to think in **sets**. SQL is built to process many rows per statement: `WHERE id IN (...)` filters by a list, `JOIN` combines related tables, and aggregates such as `SUM` and `COUNT` (with `GROUP BY`) summarise inside the database. One statement, one round trip, whatever N is.

## How Go does it

`database/sql` does not batch or hide your queries: each `QueryRow` or `Query` call is a separate statement. So the shape of your Go code *is* the shape of your database traffic, and a query inside a `for` loop is the warning sign.

Here is N+1 on a blog: one query per post to fetch its author.

```go
for i := range posts {
    db.QueryRow(`SELECT name FROM authors WHERE id = ?`, posts[i].AuthorID).
        Scan(&posts[i].Author)
}
```

The set-based version lets a `JOIN` pair every post with its author in one statement:

```go
rows, err := db.Query(`
    SELECT p.title, a.name
    FROM posts p JOIN authors a ON a.id = p.author_id
    ORDER BY p.id`)
```

The `rows.Next()` loop that follows is fine: it reads results already produced by that single query, not N more queries.

When the list comes from Go, an `IN` clause needs one `?` per element and the values go in the arguments after the SQL. The SQL text then depends on how long the list is, but the values still never enter it.

## What is special or tricky

- A placeholder binds one scalar value. `WHERE id IN (?)` given a whole slice does not expand into a list.
- The arguments parameter of `Exec`, `Query` and `QueryRow` is `...any`. You can spread a `[]any` with `slice...`, but a `[]int` is not a `[]any`: the compiler rejects it with `cannot use ids (variable of type []int) as []any value`.
- An empty `IN ()` list is a syntax error in most databases, so decide what an empty input means before building the query.
- `SUM` over zero matching rows returns `NULL`, not 0, and scanning `NULL` into an `int` fails. `COALESCE(SUM(x), 0)` turns it into 0.
- SQLite runs in-process, so its round trips are cheap and N+1 hurts less there. Code that feels fast against SQLite on a laptop can crawl against a database server across a network; the habit matters more than the local timing.
- When unsure, count statements: a counter or a log line per query makes N+1 visible.

## What you will practise

You will run the N+1 loop on purpose and count its queries, then fold the same work into one `IN (...)` query and into one streamed `Query`. The challenge checks that you compute a total with exactly one query.
units.title: The N+1 query problem
units.intro:
A loop that runs one query per id is the N+1 anti-pattern: for N ids you pay N round
trips (plus the one that produced the ids). Folding them into a single `IN (...)`
query is dramatically faster. You will count the queries both ways and then return a
total using exactly one query.

steps.title: One query, not N
steps.intro:
Each database round trip has a cost. Doing one per item inside a loop multiplies that
cost by N. A single set-based query does the same work in one trip.
steps.body:
## N+1 vs a single query

```go
// N+1: one query per id (slow)
for _, id := range ids {
    db.QueryRow(`SELECT price FROM orders WHERE id = ?`, id).Scan(&p)
    total += p
}

// One query for all ids (fast)
db.QueryRow(`SELECT SUM(price) FROM orders WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3)`).Scan(&total)
```

- The loop issues **N** separate queries — the classic N+1 pattern.
- The set-based version makes **one** round trip with an `IN (...)` list.
- Build the `IN` list from `?` placeholders (one per id) and pass the ids as
  arguments — never concatenate values into the SQL.
- Fewer round trips is usually the single biggest database win in a service.

units.concepts:
## The idea

No screen shows a million rows at once. **Pagination** splits a sorted result into pages, and two techniques dominate.

**OFFSET pagination** numbers the pages: page 3 with size 20 means "skip 40 rows, return 20". It is easy to understand and can jump to any page. But the database cannot teleport to row 40 000: it must produce and discard every skipped row, so the cost grows with the offset, roughly O(offset + size). Deep pages get slower and slower.

**Keyset pagination** (also called seek or cursor pagination) remembers *where you stopped* instead of *how many you skipped*. The client sends back the sort key of the last row it saw, and the next query asks for rows after that key. If the key is indexed, the database walks its B-tree straight to that point, an O(log n) seek, and then reads `size` rows. Page 1 and page 5 000 cost about the same.

Keyset also copes better with changing data. With OFFSET, a row inserted or deleted before the current position shifts everything, so the reader sees a row twice or misses one. A keyset cursor is anchored to a value, not to a position.

The trade-offs: keyset needs a **unique, stable sort order**, cannot jump to an arbitrary page number, and moves one page at a time.

## How Go does it

Both are plain SQL with bound parameters; `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` accept `?` like any other value. You read the page with the usual `Query` and `rows.Next()` loop, collecting values into a slice.

When the sort column is not unique, add a tie-breaker so the order is total. SQLite supports **row values**, which compare tuples left to right, so a two-column cursor stays tidy:

```go
rows, err := db.Query(`
    SELECT id, created_at, title FROM posts
    WHERE (created_at, id) > (?, ?)
    ORDER BY created_at, id
    LIMIT ?`, lastCreated, lastID, 20)
```

An index on `(created_at, id)` lets this seek directly. After reading the page, the last row's `created_at` and `id` become the cursor for the next request, often wrapped in an opaque token for the client.

## What is special or tricky

- Without `ORDER BY`, SQL promises no order at all, and pages can overlap or skip rows. Always order by the same key you filter on.
- Use `>` (strictly greater), not `>=`, or the last row of one page comes back as the first row of the next.
- The first page has no last key yet. With positive integer ids, starting from 0 works; in general you need a sentinel value or a separate first-page query.
- A slice declared as `var page []int` is `nil` until you append to it. A `nil` slice and an empty one both have length 0, but they encode differently in JSON (`null` versus `[]`), which matters when an API returns the page.
- In SQLite a negative `LIMIT` means "no limit", so validate the page size before querying.
- Check `rows.Err()` after the loop; otherwise a page cut short by an error looks like a normal short page.

## What you will practise

You will fetch the same page with `LIMIT/OFFSET` and with a keyset query, then advance a keyset cursor to the following page. The challenge asks you to build a small keyset pager that handles its edge cases.
units.title: Pagination: OFFSET vs keyset
units.intro:
Listing results a page at a time has two common shapes. `LIMIT/OFFSET` is simple but
gets slower as the offset grows, because the database still walks the skipped rows.
Keyset pagination (`WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ?`) remembers the last id and jumps
straight past it. You will build both and then a keyset pager.

steps.title: OFFSET vs keyset
steps.intro:
Both approaches return a page of rows. The difference is what happens deep into the
list: OFFSET re-scans the skipped rows, keyset seeks directly using the last id.
steps.body:
## Two ways to page

```go
// OFFSET: skip the first (page*size) rows
db.Query(`SELECT id FROM items ORDER BY id LIMIT ? OFFSET ?`, size, page*size)

// Keyset: continue after the last id you saw
db.Query(`SELECT id FROM items WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ?`, lastID, size)
```

- **`LIMIT ? OFFSET ?`** is easy, but a large `OFFSET` makes the database count past
  all the skipped rows every time.
- **Keyset** carries the last id forward; with an index on `id` it seeks straight to
  the next page, so cost stays flat as you go deeper.
- Keyset needs a stable sort key (here the primary key `id`) and `ORDER BY` on it.
- The trade-off: OFFSET can jump to any page number; keyset only moves forward from a
  known row.
