steps.title: Implement PageAfter
steps.intro:
Build a keyset pager. Given the last id a client saw and a page size, return the next
`size` ids strictly greater than it, in ascending order.
steps.instructions:
## Your turn

Implement the function `PageAfter`:

```go
func PageAfter(lastID, size int) []int { ... }
```

Seed a table with ids `1..100`, then return the next `size` ids with
`SELECT id FROM items WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ?`. Return an empty (non-nil is
fine) slice when there is nothing after `lastID` or when `size <= 0`.

Examples:

- `PageAfter(0, 3)` -> `[1 2 3]`
- `PageAfter(98, 5)` -> `[99 100]`
- `PageAfter(100, 5)` -> `[]`

Hidden tests decide correctness.

gabarito.justification:
The query reads at most `size` rows and the result slice holds at most `size` ids, so
both time and space are **O(size)** — independent of how deep into the table the page
sits. That flat cost is the whole advantage of keyset over a large `OFFSET`.

units.concepts:
## The idea

Without help, finding the rows where `email = 'b@x'` means reading every row and testing it: a **full table scan**, O(n). An **index** is a separate, sorted structure holding the values of one or more columns, each entry pointing back to its row. Because it is sorted, the database can find a value the way you find a word in a dictionary.

SQLite, like most databases, stores indexes as **B-trees**: wide, shallow trees whose nodes each hold many sorted keys. Finding a key takes O(log n) node visits, and with hundreds of keys per node even millions of rows need only a few. The leaves are in order, so ranges (`BETWEEN`, `>`, `ORDER BY`) are cheap too. The table itself is also a B-tree, keyed by its `rowid` (or its `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`).

A typical indexed lookup finds the matching rowids in the index, then fetches each row from the table. If every column the query needs is already in the index, that second step is skipped: a **covering index**.

Indexes are not free. Each one takes space, and every `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` must update every index on the table. Index the columns your queries actually filter, join or sort on.

The **query planner** decides whether to use an index. **`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`** asks it to describe its choice without running the query.

## How Go does it

Indexes are plain SQL, run with `Exec`, and your queries do not change at all: the planner picks the index on its own.

```go
db.Exec(`CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date ON orders(customer_id, created_at)`)
db.Exec(`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email)`)
```

A `UNIQUE` index also enforces a rule: inserting a duplicate email fails with a constraint error.

To Go, `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` is an ordinary query. In SQLite it returns rows of four columns (`id`, `parent`, `notused`, `detail`), and `detail` is the text to read. Typical details:

- `SCAN users`: a full table scan.
- `SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_users_email (email=?)`: a seek through the index, then a fetch of each row.
- `SEARCH users USING COVERING INDEX idx_users_email (email=?)`: the index alone answers the query.
- `SEARCH users USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)`: a lookup by the table's own key.

## What is special or tricky

- A composite index on `(customer_id, created_at)` helps queries that filter on `customer_id`, or on both columns, but not on `created_at` alone, because it is sorted by the first column first (the **leftmost prefix** rule).
- Wrapping the column in a function, as in `WHERE lower(email) = ?`, hides it from a plain index on `email`. So does a leading wildcard such as `LIKE '%x'`.
- The wording of `detail` varies between SQLite versions (older ones printed `SCAN TABLE users`). Match stable words like `SCAN` or `USING INDEX`, never the whole string.
- `USING COVERING INDEX` contains the word `INDEX` but not the exact phrase `USING INDEX`.
- `Scan` needs one destination per column, so reading a plan row takes four variables even if you only want the last one.
- Plain `EXPLAIN`, without `QUERY PLAN`, is different: it lists the low-level bytecode program, not the strategy.

## What you will practise

You will watch a `SCAN` become `USING INDEX` once an index exists, and use an index for a real lookup. The challenge asks you to confirm from Go, by reading the plan, that a lookup really uses its index.
units.title: Indexes & EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
units.intro:
An index is a sorted structure that turns a full-table scan into a quick seek. Without
one, a `WHERE col = ?` lookup scans every row; with an index on that column, SQLite
seeks straight to the match. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` shows which strategy the database
chose, so you can confirm an index is actually used.

steps.title: Why indexes matter
steps.intro:
A lookup without an index is a linear SCAN. An index on the filtered column lets the
database jump to the rows it needs. `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` reveals which one happens.
steps.body:
## Create an index, read the plan

```go
db.Exec(`CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email)`)

rows, _ := db.Query(`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT name FROM users WHERE email = ?`, "a@x")
for rows.Next() {
    var id, parent, notused int
    var detail string
    rows.Scan(&id, &parent, &notused, &detail)
    // detail: "SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_users_email (email=?)"
}
```

- **`CREATE INDEX`** builds a sorted lookup structure on one or more columns.
- Without an index, the plan says **`SCAN`** — every row is examined.
- With a matching index, the plan says **`SEARCH ... USING INDEX`** — a direct seek.
- **`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`** returns rows whose last column (`detail`) is the
  human-readable strategy; read it to verify your index is doing its job.

steps.title: No index means a SCAN
steps.intro:
With no index on the filtered column, SQLite has to examine every row. `EXPLAIN QUERY
PLAN` says so — its detail text contains `SCAN`.
steps.prompt:

steps.target:
package main

import (
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"
	"strings"

	_ "modernc.org/sqlite"
)

func main() {
	db, _ := sql.Open("sqlite", ":memory:")
	defer db.Close()
	db.Exec(`CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, v TEXT)`)
	db.Exec(`INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b')`)
	rows, _ := db.Query(`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT v FROM t WHERE v = ?`, "a")
	defer rows.Close()
	plan := ""
	for rows.Next() {
		var a, b, c int
		var d string
		rows.Scan(&a, &b, &c, &d)
		plan += d
	}
	fmt.Println(strings.Contains(plan, "SCAN"))
}

units.concepts:
## The idea

**Concurrency** means structuring a program as several independent activities whose lifetimes overlap. **Parallelism** means those activities really execute at the same instant on different CPU cores. Concurrency is about *structure*; parallelism is about *execution*. A well-structured concurrent program runs in parallel whenever the hardware allows it.

Most systems express concurrency with **threads**: flows of control scheduled by the operating system, each with its own large stack. Threads are costly to create and to switch between, because every switch goes through the kernel. Go uses **goroutines** instead: tasks with tiny stacks (a few kilobytes that grow on demand), scheduled by the Go runtime onto a small pool of OS threads. This is called **M:N scheduling**: many goroutines, few threads.

Starting work concurrently is a **fork**. Sooner or later you must **join**: wait until the forked work has finished before you use its results or exit. A `sync.WaitGroup` is a counting join: a counter of outstanding tasks plus a way to block until it reaches zero.

## How Go does it

Prefix any function call with `go`. The arguments are evaluated immediately, in the calling goroutine; the function body runs later, concurrently.

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"sync"
)

func greet(name string, wg *sync.WaitGroup) {
	defer wg.Done()
	fmt.Println("hello,", name)
}

func main() {
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	for _, name := range []string{"ana", "rui", "eva"} {
		wg.Add(1)
		go greet(name, &wg)
	}
	wg.Wait()
}
```

Notice that `greet` receives a **pointer** to the WaitGroup. The zero value of `sync.WaitGroup` is ready to use; you never call a constructor.

Since Go 1.22, each iteration of a `for` loop gets a fresh loop variable, so a closure that captures `name` sees its own value. Before 1.22 all closures shared one variable and often saw only the last value, which is why passing the value as an argument, as the drills do, is a common and explicit habit.

## What is special or tricky

- **`main` does not wait.** When `main` returns, the program exits and running goroutines are simply dropped. `time.Sleep` is not synchronisation; it only makes the bug rarer.
- **Call `Add` before the `go` statement**, not inside the goroutine. Otherwise `Wait` may run first, see zero, and return early.
- **Never copy a WaitGroup.** Passing it by value gives the goroutine its own counter, so `Wait` never sees the `Done`. `go vet` reports this as passing a lock by value.
- More `Done` calls than `Add` panics with `sync: negative WaitGroup counter`. A `Wait` that nobody will ever release ends with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`.
- **Output order is not deterministic.** Prints from goroutines interleave differently each run. If you need a reproducible *result*, design for it: let each goroutine write to its own slot, then combine the slots after `Wait`.
- Two goroutines writing the same variable without synchronisation is a **data race**. Run `go run -race .` to have the race detector look for it.

## What you will practise

You will launch goroutines with a WaitGroup, collect results into disjoint slots, and split a slice across a fixed number of workers. The challenge asks you to combine those ideas into a parallel computation whose answer is the same on every run.
units.title: Goroutines & WaitGroup
units.intro:
The foundation of Go concurrency. A **goroutine** is a function that runs
concurrently, multiplexed by the Go runtime onto a small pool of OS threads — so
cheap you can launch thousands, where native threads would cost you megabytes
each. Launching one is just `go f()`. But a goroutine runs *independently*: if
`main` returns, the program ends and in-flight goroutines are dropped. A
`sync.WaitGroup` is the counter that lets `main` wait for a batch of goroutines to
finish. You will launch goroutines, coordinate them, and finish by summing a slice
across several of them — with a deterministic result.

steps.title: Goroutines vs threads, and WaitGroup
steps.intro:
Goroutines are not OS threads: the runtime schedules many goroutines onto few
threads, so they are cheap to create and switch. Because they run independently of
`main`, you need an explicit way to wait for them — that is what a WaitGroup does.
steps.body:
## Goroutines

```go
go doWork()        // runs doWork concurrently, returns immediately
go func() { ... }() // or an anonymous function, launched at once
```

A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime, not the OS. Starting
one with `go` returns instantly; the work happens alongside the rest of your
program. The catch: when `main` returns, the whole program exits — any goroutine
still running is abandoned.

## WaitGroup: wait for a batch

```go
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
    wg.Add(1)              // one more goroutine to wait for
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()    // mark this one done on return
        work()
    }()
}
wg.Wait()                  // block until the counter reaches zero
```

Three calls do all the work: **`Add(n)`** raises the counter, **`Done()`** lowers
it by one (put it in a `defer` so it always runs), and **`Wait()`** blocks until
the counter hits zero. This is how `main` holds on until every goroutine finishes.

## Passing the loop value

When you launch a goroutine inside a loop, pass the loop value as an **argument**
so each goroutine gets its own copy:

```go
go func(n int) { use(n) }(i)
```

## A trick for lock-free results

If each goroutine writes to a **different slot** of a shared slice
(`results[i] = ...`), no two goroutines ever touch the same memory, so you need no
lock at all. You will use this to collect partial sums.

steps.title: Launch goroutines, wait with a WaitGroup
steps.intro:
Each iteration registers one goroutine with `Add(1)` and launches it; `defer
wg.Done()` marks it finished on return; `wg.Wait()` holds `main` until all three
are done, so the final line is guaranteed to print last.
steps.prompt: Launch three goroutines and use a `sync.WaitGroup` so `main` waits for all of them.

Registers one more goroutine before starting it.
Starts a goroutine running an anonymous function; `n` is its own copy of `i`.
`defer` guarantees `Done` runs on return, decrementing the counter.
The goroutine's work: print its number.
Closes and calls the anonymous function with the current `i`.
Blocks until the counter hits zero — all three goroutines finished.
Prints a final line, guaranteed after every goroutine.
steps.explanation:
`Add`/`Done`/`Wait` are the whole protocol. The three worker lines may print in any
order — that is concurrency — but the final line always prints last, because
`Wait` blocks until the count returns to zero.

steps.title: Collect results without a lock
steps.intro:
Each goroutine writes to its own slot of the `results` slice, so no two goroutines
ever touch the same memory — disjoint writes need no mutex. `main` reads the slice
only after `Wait` returns.
steps.prompt: Square four numbers concurrently, each goroutine writing into its own slice slot.
line_comments: The input: a slice of four numbers.
A results slice of the same length — each goroutine owns one slot.
A WaitGroup to wait for every goroutine.
Loops over the slice with index and value.
Launches a goroutine; `idx` and `val` are its own copies.
Writes only to slot `idx` — no two goroutines share a slot, so no lock is needed.
Closes and calls the goroutine with this index and value.
Waits for all goroutines to finish.
steps.explanation:
Writing to disjoint indices is the simplest safe way to gather concurrent results:
no shared mutable cell, so no data race. The output `[100 400 900 1600]` is always
in order, because slot `i` is always written by the goroutine that owns index `i`.

steps.title: Sum a slice with a fixed worker count
steps.intro:
A preview of the challenge. Three workers split the slice by striding — worker
`id` handles indices id, id+3, id+6, ... — each keeping a private running sum, then
`main` combines the partials after `Wait`.
steps.prompt: Add up a slice using three workers, each summing every third element.
line_comments: A fixed number of workers to divide the work among.
One result slot per worker — again, disjoint slots mean no lock.
`Add` the whole count once, instead of one at a time.
Each worker gets its own id.
A private running sum for this worker.
Strided loop: worker `id` handles indices id, id+workers, id+2*workers, ...
Stores this worker's partial sum in its own slot.
Closes and calls the worker goroutine.
Waits for every worker to finish.
Now combine the partials on the main goroutine.
Adds each partial into the total.
steps.explanation:
Striding splits the work evenly without any shared counter: each worker reads its
own indices and writes its own slot. Summing the partials afterwards is sequential
and tiny. The total `21` is deterministic because addition does not care which
worker finished first.

## Your turn

```go
func SumParallel(nums []int) int { ... }
```

Return the sum of all integers in `nums`, computed with the help of several
goroutines coordinated by a `sync.WaitGroup`. The result must be correct and
deterministic regardless of goroutine scheduling.

Examples:

- `SumParallel([]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5})` → `15`
- `SumParallel(nil)` → `0`

**Hint:** give each worker a disjoint share of the slice (for example by striding),
let it compute a private partial sum into its own slot, `Wait` for all of them, then
add the partials. Addition is commutative, so order never matters.

Hidden tests decide correctness. Implement it, then submit.

gabarito.justification:
Every element is visited exactly once across the workers, so the work is **O(n)**;
the only extra memory is one partial-sum slot per worker, a fixed count, so the
extra space is **O(1)**. Each worker owns a disjoint stride of indices and its own
output slot, so there is no shared mutable state and no lock — and because addition
is commutative, the total is identical no matter which goroutine the runtime runs
first. That is what makes the result deterministic.

units.concepts:
## The idea

Goroutines need a way to exchange data. One option is shared memory guarded by locks. Go favours another model, **CSP** (Communicating Sequential Processes, Tony Hoare, 1978): independent processes share nothing and talk by passing messages over **channels**. The Go proverb sums it up: *do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.*

A channel is a typed, goroutine-safe **FIFO queue** with blocking behaviour. Sending a value hands it from one goroutine to another, so only one side works on it at a time. Two shapes matter:

- **Unbuffered**: a synchronous handoff. Sender and receiver must meet (a *rendezvous*), so the exchange also synchronises them.
- **Buffered**: a bounded queue. A fast producer can run ahead by up to the capacity, then it is slowed down. That automatic slowing is called **back-pressure**.

The classic pattern built on this is **producer/consumer**, and chaining several stages gives a **pipeline**.

## How Go does it

The type is `chan T`. You create a channel with `make`, send with `ch <- v` and receive with `<-ch`. The zero value of a channel type is `nil`, which is not usable.

A channel is a natural way to return a result from a goroutine:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	done := make(chan string)
	go func() {
		done <- strings.ToUpper("finished")
	}()
	fmt.Println(<-done) // waits for the goroutine, no WaitGroup needed
}
```

`close(ch)` means "no more values". Values already in the buffer survive the close:

```go
ch := make(chan int, 1)
ch <- 5
close(ch)
v, ok := <-ch // 5 true: a buffered value is still delivered
v, ok = <-ch  // 0 false: closed and drained
```

`for v := range ch` keeps receiving until the channel is closed and drained. `len(ch)` and `cap(ch)` report how full the buffer is.

Directional types restrict a channel's use: `chan<- T` can only send, `<-chan T` can only receive. A bidirectional channel converts to either one implicitly when you pass it to a function.

## What is special or tricky

- **Deadlock.** An unbuffered send with no receiver blocks forever. If every goroutine is blocked, the runtime stops with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`. The classic case is sending and receiving in the same goroutine.
- **Close from the sending side only.** Sending on a closed channel panics with `send on closed channel`, and closing twice panics with `close of closed channel`.
- **Receiving from a closed channel never blocks.** It returns the zero value at once. Use `v, ok` when a real zero must be told apart from "closed".
- **A `range` over a channel that is never closed never ends.** Forgetting `close` turns into a deadlock or a goroutine stuck forever.
- A `nil` channel blocks forever on both send and receive, so always `make` your channels.
- Using a channel against its direction is a compile error, for example "cannot send to receive-only channel".
- Closing is a signal, not cleanup. Unreachable channels are garbage collected whether or not they were closed.

## What you will practise

You will meet the rendezvous, fill and drain a buffered channel, and wire a producer to a consumer with directional types. The challenge asks you to build that same producer/consumer shape yourself.
units.title: Channels
units.intro:
Channels are how goroutines **communicate** — Go's motto is *"don't communicate by
sharing memory; share memory by communicating."* A channel is a typed pipe: one
goroutine sends values in, another receives them out, and the channel handles the
synchronisation. You will learn unbuffered channels (a send and a receive meet, a
rendezvous), buffered channels (a small queue), how `close` signals "no more
values", and how `range` drains a channel until it closes. The unit ends with a
producer/consumer pipeline that sums a stream of numbers.

steps.title: Sending, receiving, closing, ranging
steps.intro:
A channel carries values of one type between goroutines and synchronises them while
doing it. Unbuffered channels pair a send with a receive; buffered channels hold a
few values; closing a channel tells receivers the stream has ended.
steps.body:
## Make, send, receive

```go
ch := make(chan int)   // unbuffered channel of ints
ch <- 7                // send 7 (blocks until a receiver is ready)
v := <-ch              // receive (blocks until a value is ready)
```

On an **unbuffered** channel a send blocks until some goroutine receives, and a
receive blocks until some goroutine sends — the two meet at a single point, a
*rendezvous*. That rendezvous is itself the synchronisation.

## Buffered channels

```go
ch := make(chan int, 3)  // room for three values
ch <- 1; ch <- 2; ch <- 3 // these do not block: there is room
```

A **buffered** channel holds up to its capacity without a waiting receiver. Sends
block only when the buffer is full; receives block only when it is empty.

## Close and range

```go
close(ch)             // no more values will be sent
for v := range ch {   // yields buffered values, then stops at close
    use(v)
}

v, ok := <-ch         // ok == false once the channel is closed and drained
```

**`close`** marks a channel finished. A `range` over a channel reads values until it
is closed and drained, then ends the loop. The two-value receive `v, ok := <-ch`
reports whether a real value came (`ok` true) or the channel is closed (`ok` false).
Only the **sender** should close a channel, and never send on a closed one.

## Directional channels

A parameter typed `chan<- int` may only **send**; `<-chan int` may only **receive**.
It documents and enforces a goroutine's role.

steps.title: An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous
steps.intro:
The goroutine's send blocks until `main` receives; `main`'s receive blocks until the
goroutine sends. They meet at one point — that handshake both moves the value and
synchronises the two goroutines.
steps.prompt: Send a value from a goroutine and receive it in `main` over an unbuffered channel.
line_comments: Makes an unbuffered channel of ints — a send waits for a matching receive.
Launches a goroutine, so the send has someone to pair with.
Sends 42; it blocks here until `main` receives.
Closes and calls the anonymous goroutine.
Receives from the channel — the moment the send completes, a rendezvous.
steps.explanation:
If you sent on an unbuffered channel from the only goroutine, the program would
deadlock — nobody to receive. Launching a goroutine gives the send a partner; the
two block until they meet, which is exactly how channels synchronise work.

steps.title: Buffer, close, and range
steps.intro:
A buffered channel takes three values without a receiver; `close` marks the end;
`range` then yields them in first-in-first-out order and stops cleanly at the close.
steps.prompt: Fill a buffered channel, close it, and drain it with `range` — in FIFO order.
line_comments: A buffered channel holding up to 3 ints — sends do not block while there is room.
Sends 1 into the buffer (no receiver needed yet).
Sends 3 — the buffer is now full.
`close` says no more values will be sent.
`range` over a channel yields buffered values in FIFO order, then stops at close.
Prints each value: 1, 2, 3 — always in that order.
Closes the loop (it ends when the channel is drained and closed).
steps.explanation:
Buffering lets a sender run ahead of a receiver by up to the capacity. Closing is
what lets `range` terminate — without it, the loop would block forever waiting for a
fourth value. The output order is deterministic: a channel is a FIFO queue.

steps.title: Directional channels in a pipeline
steps.intro:
The `produce` function is typed `chan<- int`, so it may only send — the compiler

## The idea

A goroutine often has several possible events to wait for: a result on one channel, a message on another, a deadline passing. Waiting on just one of them in sequence can hang the program while the other is ready. **Multiplexing** means waiting on all of them at once and reacting to whichever is ready first, much like the Unix `select`/`poll` calls for files and sockets.

A **timeout** is one of those events: "stop waiting after *d*". Timeouts keep a slow or dead partner from blocking you forever.

When several events are ready at the same moment, the choice between them is **non-deterministic**. A correct concurrent program does not depend on the order of arrivals. Instead it maintains an **invariant**, a fact that stays true for any interleaving, such as "the total equals the sum of everything received".

## How Go does it

`select` looks like a `switch`, but each `case` is a channel send or receive. It blocks until one case can proceed and runs exactly that case. If several are ready, it picks one at random. A `default` case makes the `select` non-blocking.

`time.After(d)` returns a channel that delivers one value after `d`, so a deadline becomes just another case:

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	slow := make(chan string, 1) // buffered: the late sender can still finish
	go func() {
		time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
		slow <- "done"
	}()
	select {
	case msg := <-slow:
		fmt.Println(msg)
	case <-time.After(10 * time.Millisecond):
		fmt.Println("gave up waiting")
	}
}
```

With `default`, you can try an operation without blocking:

```go
select {
case jobs <- task:
	fmt.Println("queued")
default:
	fmt.Println("queue full, dropping task")
}
```

## What is special or tricky

- **A closed channel is always ready.** Its receive case fires again and again with zero values, so a `select` loop over a closed channel spins and miscounts. Use the two-value receive to notice the close and retire that case.
- **A `nil` channel is never ready.** Its case is effectively switched off. That is why setting a variable to `nil` disables a case. A `select` where every channel is `nil` and there is no `default` blocks forever. So does an empty `select {}`.
- **`break` inside a `select` leaves only the `select`**, not the surrounding `for`. To exit the loop, use a labelled `break`, `return`, or a loop condition.
- **`time.After` in a loop creates a new timer on every iteration.** That gives you a per-iteration idle timeout. For one overall deadline, call it once before the loop and keep the channel.
- **Goroutine leaks.** In the timeout example, an unbuffered `slow` would leave the sleeping goroutine blocked on its send forever, because nobody receives any more. A buffer of one lets it finish.
- If your output depends on which ready case runs first, your program is flaky. Make the result depend only on the invariant.

## What you will practise

You will use `select` over two ready channels, add a `time.After` timeout, and merge two channels until both close. The challenge asks you to merge two producers with a `select` loop and compute a total that does not depend on arrival order.

steps.body:
## select

```go
select {
case v := <-a:
    useA(v)
case v := <-b:
    useB(v)
}
```

`select` blocks until **one** of its cases can run, then runs exactly that case. If
several are ready, it picks one at random — so never rely on *which* case fires,
only on the invariant you maintain (for example, a running total).

## Timeouts with time.After

```go
select {
case v := <-work:
    use(v)
case <-time.After(2 * time.Second):
    fmt.Println("timed out")
}
```

`time.After(d)` returns a `<-chan Time` that receives a value after `d` elapses.
Put it in a `select` and whichever happens first — the work or the deadline — wins.

## Draining until closed: the nil-channel idiom

A receive on a **nil** channel blocks forever, so a nil case in a `select` is simply
never chosen. That gives a clean way to merge channels until each closes:

```go
for a != nil || b != nil {
    select {
    case v, ok := <-a:
        if !ok { a = nil; continue } // closed: disable this case
        use(v)
    case v, ok := <-b:
        if !ok { b = nil; continue }
        use(v)
    }
}
```

When a channel closes, set its variable to `nil` so its case stops being selected;
the loop ends once both are nil. The *order* of arrivals varies, but a total you
accumulate does not.

units.concepts:
## The idea

When goroutines share memory, a **race condition** can appear: the result depends on how their steps interleave. The most dangerous form is a **data race**: two goroutines access the same memory location at the same time, at least one of them writes, and nothing orders the accesses. `counter++` looks atomic but is really three steps (read, add, write), so two goroutines can both read the same old value and one increment is lost.

The fix is **mutual exclusion**. You protect a **critical section** so that only one goroutine runs it at a time. Locks also establish a **happens-before** order: everything done before an `Unlock` is visible to the goroutine that takes the lock next. Without such synchronisation, one goroutine may not see another's writes at all.

**Atomic operations** are the smallest tool: single read-modify-write steps that the hardware makes indivisible. **Worker pools** add *bounded concurrency*: a fixed number N of workers drain a shared job queue, so a million jobs never means a million simultaneous goroutines. Spreading jobs out is called *fan-out*, and gathering results back into one stream is *fan-in*.

## How Go does it

`sync.Mutex` has `Lock` and `Unlock`, and its zero value is an unlocked mutex. The idiom is to keep the mutex next to the data it guards and to unlock with `defer`:

```go
type Inventory struct {
	mu    sync.Mutex
	stock map[string]int
}

func (inv *Inventory) Add(item string, n int) {
	inv.mu.Lock()
	defer inv.mu.Unlock()
	inv.stock[item] += n
}
```

`sync.RWMutex` lets many readers in at once (`RLock`/`RUnlock`) but only one writer. For a lone counter, `sync/atomic` offers `atomic.AddInt64(&n, 1)` and `atomic.LoadInt64(&n)`, and since Go 1.19 the typed `atomic.Int64`, with `Add` and `Load` methods.

A worker pool in Go has four parts:

- a jobs channel that every worker ranges over;
- a results channel that every worker sends to;
- a `sync.WaitGroup` that counts the workers;
- a small extra goroutine that waits on the group and then closes the results channel.

That extra goroutine matters. If the collecting goroutine itself called `Wait` before reading results, the workers would block on their sends and the program would deadlock.

## What is special or tricky

- **Maps are not safe for concurrent writes.** The runtime often catches it and crashes with `fatal error: concurrent map writes`.
- **Go mutexes are not reentrant.** Calling `Lock` twice in the same goroutine deadlocks it.
- **Do not copy a mutex.** A struct holding a `sync.Mutex` must be used through a pointer, with pointer receivers. `go vet` flags copies.
- **Forgetting `Unlock` on an early return** freezes every other goroutine. `defer` prevents it.
- **Mixing atomic and plain access is still a race.** If you write with `atomic.AddInt64`, read with `atomic.LoadInt64`.
- The race detector (`go run -race .`) reports `WARNING: DATA RACE`, but only for races that actually occur during that run. A silent run is evidence, not proof.
- Choose N on purpose. For CPU-bound work, `runtime.NumCPU()` is a sensible start.

## What you will practise

You will guard a counter with a `Mutex`, build a three-worker pool, and replace the lock with `sync/atomic`. The challenge asks you to answer a counting question with a worker pool, deterministically.

units.intro:
Sometimes goroutines really must share one piece of memory — a counter, a map, an
accumulator. Then you need **mutual exclusion**: a `sync.Mutex` whose `Lock`/`Unlock`
lets only one goroutine into the critical section at a time, so updates are not
lost. For simple counters, `sync/atomic` does the same lock-free. And the canonical

steps.title: Mutex, atomic, and the worker-pool pattern
steps.intro:
When goroutines share mutable memory, concurrent writes race and updates get lost. A
`sync.Mutex` serialises access to a critical section; `sync/atomic` does it lock-free
for single integers. A worker pool bounds how many goroutines run at once.
steps.body:
## The problem: a data race

Two goroutines running `counter++` can read the same old value and both write back
`old+1`, losing one increment. The `-race` detector flags exactly this.

## sync.Mutex

```go
var mu sync.Mutex
mu.Lock()
counter++        // critical section: exactly one goroutine at a time
mu.Unlock()
```

`Lock` blocks until the mutex is free, then this goroutine owns it; `Unlock` releases
it. Only one goroutine holds the lock at once, so the increment is safe. Keep the
critical section small, and never forget to `Unlock` (a `defer mu.Unlock()` is common).

## sync/atomic

```go
var n int64
atomic.AddInt64(&n, 1)      // safe increment, no lock
total := atomic.LoadInt64(&n)
```

For a single counter, an atomic operation is simpler and faster than a mutex: the
hardware guarantees the read-modify-write happens as one indivisible step.

## Worker pool

Launch a fixed number of workers, each ranging over a shared **jobs** channel and
sending to a **results** channel:

```go
jobs := make(chan int)
results := make(chan int)
for w := 0; w < N; w++ {
    go func() {
        for j := range jobs { results <- process(j) }
    }()
}
```

Feed jobs, `close(jobs)` when done, and in a separate goroutine `wg.Wait()` then
`close(results)` so the collector's `range` can finish. A pool bounds concurrency to
`N` no matter how many jobs arrive — the standard shape for parallel work in Go.

than 100. The mutex serialises the critical section, so every increment lands. Run

units.concepts:
## The idea

An **abstract data type** is defined by its operations, not by how it is stored. Two of the most useful ones restrict *where* elements enter and leave:

- A **stack** is **LIFO** (last in, first out), with `push`, `pop` and `peek` at one end. It models anything nested or reversible: the call stack of a running program, undo history, depth-first search, and nested structure in text, where whatever opened most recently must close first.
- A **queue** is **FIFO** (first in, first out): `enqueue` at the back, `dequeue` at the front. It models fairness and waiting: task scheduling, buffers, breadth-first search.

A good implementation makes every one of these operations **O(1)**, meaning constant time no matter how many elements are stored.

## How Go does it

Go has no built-in stack or queue type, because a **slice** already does the job. A slice is a small header (pointer, length, capacity) over a backing array:

- `append` adds at the end in **amortised O(1)**. When capacity runs out, it allocates a bigger array and copies, but that happens rarely enough that the average cost per push stays constant.
- Reslicing (`s[:len(s)-1]` or `s[1:]`) is O(1). It only moves the header and never copies elements.

Wrapping the slice in a type gives a safer API. With generics (Go 1.18+), one definition serves every element type:

```go
type Stack[T any] struct {
	items []T
}

func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T) { s.items = append(s.items, v) }

func (s *Stack[T]) Pop() (T, bool) {
	var zero T
	if len(s.items) == 0 {
		return zero, false
	}
	v := s.items[len(s.items)-1]
	s.items = s.items[:len(s.items)-1]
	return v, true
}
```

The methods use a **pointer receiver** because `append` and reslicing produce a new header that must be stored back. Returning `(T, bool)` is the comma-ok style: the caller learns about an empty stack without a crash.

## What is special or tricky

- **Popping an empty slice panics**: `panic: runtime error: index out of range [-1]`. Always check `len` first.
- **`append` returns the new slice.** Writing `append(stack, x)` on its own line is a compile error ("value ... is not used"). Always assign: `stack = append(stack, x)`.
- **Slices share backing arrays.** After `b := a`, both point to the same memory. Popping from one and pushing to it can overwrite elements the other still sees. Keep one owner per stack.
- **Dequeuing with `q[1:]` keeps the dropped elements in memory** until `append` reallocates. That is fine for short-lived queues. For long-lived ones, use a ring buffer or `container/list`. Between goroutines, a buffered channel is already a FIFO queue.
- **Strings are bytes; ranging gives runes.** `s[i]` is a `byte`, while `for _, r := range s` yields `rune` values (Unicode code points). A character literal like `'('` is an untyped rune constant that compares with either.

## What you will practise

You will push and pop a stack, serve a queue in order, and reverse a slice by draining a stack. The challenge applies the LIFO idea to checking nested structure in a string.
units.title: Stacks & queues with slices
units.intro:
Two of the most useful data structures need no library at all — a Go slice is enough.
Push and pop from the right and a slice behaves as a **stack** (last in, first out);
take from the front instead and it is a **queue** (first in, first out). You will build
both, use a stack to reverse a slice, and finish by checking bracket balance — the
canonical stack problem.

steps.title: A slice is a stack and a queue
steps.intro:
`append` grows a slice on the right; reslicing shrinks it. Pop the right end and you have
a LIFO stack; take the left end and you have a FIFO queue. No container package required.
steps.body:
## Stack (LIFO)

Push with `append`, peek the last element, pop by reslicing away the last element:

```go
stack = append(stack, x)      // push
top := stack[len(stack)-1]    // peek the top
stack = stack[:len(stack)-1]  // pop
```

Last in, first out: the most recent push is the first pop.

## Queue (FIFO)

Push on the right, but take from the **front**:

```go
queue = append(queue, x)  // enqueue
front := queue[0]         // peek the front
queue = queue[1:]         // dequeue
```

First in, first out: the oldest element leaves first.

## When to reach for what

A stack models "undo", recursion, and matching brackets. A queue models work waiting in
line and breadth-first traversal. Reslicing is O(1), so both are cheap. (Reslicing a
queue's front repeatedly keeps the dropped heads in the backing array; for long-lived
queues use a ring buffer or `container/list`. For exercises, a slice is perfect.)

steps.title: Push and pop a stack
steps.intro:
Push three values onto a slice-stack, then pop one. Because the last value pushed is the
first popped, the result is fully deterministic.
steps.prompt:
Push 1, 2, 3 onto a stack, then pop the top.

**Why:** a stack is the simplest use of `append`/reslice, and its last-in-first-out order
is the backbone of bracket matching, undo stacks, and depth-first traversal.
steps.target:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    stack := []int{}
    stack = append(stack, 1)
    stack = append(stack, 2)
    stack = append(stack, 3)
    top := stack[len(stack)-1]
    stack = stack[:len(stack)-1]
    fmt.Println("popped", top, "left", stack)
}
line_comments: An empty int slice used as a stack.
Push 1 — `append` grows the slice on the right (the top).
Push 3 on top — the stack is now [1 2 3].
Peek the top: the last element.
Pop: reslice to drop the last element (LIFO).
Prints `popped 3 left [1 2]` — last in, first out.
steps.explanation:
The top of a slice-stack is its last element, so peeking is `stack[len(stack)-1]` and
popping is `stack[:len(stack)-1]`. Push 1, 2, 3 and the top is 3 — the most recent push
is the first pop. Deterministic every run.

    queue := []string{}
    queue = append(queue, "a")
    queue = append(queue, "b")
